frameworks.name: Four Pillars of Legitimate Education
frameworks.definition: A four-part framework distinguishing legitimate education businesses from scams: selective customer admission, data-backed outcomes (not income promises), free content paired with paid implementation, and willingness to fail students to protect brand.

claims.text: The primary difference between a legitimate education business (like Harvard) and a scam (like $10,000/month courses promising instant riches) is not the quality of education but four structural mechanics: selective admission, outcome data instead of income promises, free content paired with paid implementation, and willingness to exclude students who won't succeed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to educational products and courses
claims.mechanism: Selective admission filters out poor-fit customers who would leave negative reviews and claim scam; data-based outcomes over testimonials prevent setting false expectations; free content establishes thought leadership and demand; exclusion of poor performers protects long-term brand equity.

claims.text: A red flag for illegitimate education is when every applicant who submits a credit card is admitted — i.e., the only screening criteria are 'having a pulse and a credit card.' Legitimate education businesses have explicit screening metrics to identify who is not a good fit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Unqualified customers are more likely to fail, leave negative reviews, and label the business a scam. Selective admission pre-filters for high-likelihood-of-success customers, reducing churn and reputational damage.

claims.text: Legitimate education businesses publish aggregate outcome data (top 20%, average, median, disaggregated by industry/outcome) rather than cherry-picked testimonials. They do not promise outcomes within a specific timeframe (e.g., 'success in six weeks'); they report actual timelines (e.g., 'four years of study before graduated').
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Publishing raw data (median, top 20%, average) instead of sensationalized testimonials prevents false expectations and distinguishes legitimate businesses from scams.

claims.text: Legitimate education businesses monetize the curriculum (sell the content itself) rarely; instead they give away all core content for free and monetize implementation, coaching, accountability, and feedback on customer execution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Free high-quality content establishes thought leadership, demonstrates value, and attracts demand; paid implementation extracts value from serious customers and allows for accountability and personalization that free content cannot provide.

claims.text: Legitimate education brands rank-order their graduates by success level and publicly acknowledge that not everyone who pays gets the endorsement or completion status. Some students fail, and that willingness to exclude poor performers is essential to maintaining brand equity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Excluding underperformers signals that the brand standard is high and that the endorsement carries meaningful weight. This increases the value of the credential and attracts top-tier candidates in subsequent years.

claims.text: If an education business accepts only naturally-talented candidates (high selectivity on entry), removes poor performers (high selectivity on exit), sets outcome expectations based on data, and highlights student experience and network over income, it becomes harder to sell in the short term but builds long-term brand demand and pricing power.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: new education business building from scratch
seeking long-term brand equity over short-term revenue
claims.mechanism: Short-term sales difficulty is offset by virtuous cycle: high-quality graduates succeed, tell peers, attract more top-talent applicants, increasing average outcome, reinforcing brand premium. Thought-leading free content amplifies this loop.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commoditized or low-selectivity products where brand matters less than reach
Does not apply to courses designed to maximize short-term revenue at expense of long-term reputation

claims.text: Creating excess demand relative to supply (via thought-leading free content) allows an education business to keep prices high and maintain selectivity. The marketplace logic is: 'If their free content is better than competitors' paid content, their paid content must be even better.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Free superior content signals quality and builds audience; relative to that high baseline, paid offerings appear to offer even greater value. Supply scarcity (selective admission) further supports premium pricing.

claims.text: Building a legitimate education brand takes time (Hormozi estimates at least one year of consistent content production before measurable brand effects). A one-year-old education program with 25 high-performing graduates can command pricing comparable to or higher than a four-year program (like Harvard at $250,000) if the outcome data is strong and graduates' income is 5-10x industry average.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: skill training with clear income outcomes
claims.mechanism: Exceptional outcome data (top 5-20 percentile performance by graduates) justifies premium pricing independent of program duration. Peer referral from high-performing graduates creates compounding demand.

numbers.axis: time to brand establishment and pricing power

anchors.value: one-year program can charge multiples of Harvard's $250k/4-year tuition

examples.text: Alex Hormozi discusses a hypothetical sales school launched by his neighbor Jacob. If built legitimately: Jacob would give away all course material for free via various platforms, and monetize only the implementation layer—listening to sales calls, providing real-time feedback, and monitoring performance over time. The free content would establish Jacob as a thought leader; the paid service would deliver accountability and personalized coaching that free content alone cannot provide.

Harvard publishes data on graduate outcomes by industry, income percentile (top 20%, median, average), and time-to-credential (four years), rather than cherry-picking the highest earners (e.g., a Goldman Sachs analyst making $185k). This data-forward approach prevents false expectations: students know they are not going to earn $185k immediately, but have realistic expectations of the outcome distribution.

If an education business accepts only 10% of applicants (natural talent filtering), removes the bottom performers during the program (exit-based ranking), and produces graduates earning 5x the industry average for salespeople ($300k vs. $60k), the brand compounds: graduates tell peers, demand increases on both sides (inbound applicant pool and job placements), and pricing power grows because the 'one-year education' is now perceived as worth more than a generic four-year program.

practices.text: When building an education business, explicitly define screening metrics for customer fit and reject applicants who do not meet those criteria, even if they have a credit card.
Publish aggregate outcome data (median, top 20%, average, disaggregated by category) rather than hand-picked success stories or income testimonials.
Give away all core curriculum content for free across multiple platforms; monetize the implementation, coaching, feedback, and accountability layer instead.
Maintain brand standards by ranking graduates by performance and being willing to exclude poor performers from endorsement or completion, even if they paid.
Spend at least one year building thought-leading free content before expecting brand-based pricing power or selective admission to work.
